profile.name: Harsh Raj
profile.headline: DATA SCIENTIST / AI & ML
profile.intro: I design and ship machine learning systems end to end — data pipelines, honest evaluation, and models that hold up once they leave the notebook.
profile.status: Open to data science & applied ML roles
profile.bio:
I am a data scientist with five years of practice across retail, healthcare and industrial data. My work tends to start in the unglamorous middle of a problem: an undocumented table, an ambiguous question, a metric that everyone quotes but nobody has defined. I like that part.

Most of what I build ends up as a system rather than a report — a churn model wired into a CRM, a defect detector running on a factory line, a forecasting service a planning team opens every Monday. That means I care as much about evaluation harnesses, monitoring and communication as I do about model choice.

I write Python and SQL daily, read papers slowly, and keep a notebook of failed experiments so I stop repeating them. Outside of work I run short workshops on machine learning fundamentals for students and early-career analysts.
profile.approach:
Start from the decision|Before touching data I write down the decision the model is supposed to change and the cost of being wrong in each direction. Most modelling mistakes are really specification mistakes.
Build the evaluation first|A held-out set, a baseline and a metric that reflects the real cost. If the harness is honest, the model choice becomes a short conversation instead of an argument.
Earn complexity|Rules, averages and logistic regression are cheap and interpretable. I only reach for gradient boosting or a neural network when the validation curve says it pays for itself.
Design for the failure case|Silent drift and quiet distribution shift break more systems than bad accuracy. Every model I ship has monitoring, a retrain trigger and a documented fallback.
Explain it twice|Once for the engineers who have to maintain it, once for the people who have to trust it. If I cannot explain a model in two registers, it is not ready.

projects.title: Churn Signal
projects.summary: A retention engine that predicts which subscribers will leave in the next 60 days and explains why, wired into the CRM the retention team already uses.
projects.overview:
Churn Signal is a production scoring service for a subscription media platform with 410k active accounts. It produces a 60-day churn probability per account every night, ranks the drivers behind each score, and pushes the result into the CRM as a queue the retention team works through each morning.

The interesting part of the project was not the classifier. It was rebuilding the label. The original churn definition counted anyone who cancelled, which quietly described customers who had already decided to leave weeks earlier, so the outreach always arrived too late.
projects.problem: Retention was spending its budget on the loudest customers rather than the ones most likely to leave. There was no prioritised list, offers were sent by tenure cohort, and the team could not tell whether a save attempt had worked.
projects.approach: I redefined churn as activity decay rather than cancellation, moving the prediction window back to 60 days before the event. Feature work covered tenure, engagement decay curves, payment behaviour, support contact sentiment and plan-change history. After a season-based rolling validation, gradient boosting won over a logistic baseline, and SHAP values generated the per-account reason codes the retention team now reads.
projects.datasetInfo: 410k accounts, 26 months of event-level engagement data, 4.2M support interactions and 88 behavioural features after aggregation. Training set: 318k labelled accounts; validation used three seasonal folds to avoid leakage from the pandemic-era retention spike.
projects.modelInfo: XGBoost classifier with 420 estimators, depth 6, class-weighted for the 11% positive rate. Hyperparameters tuned with Optuna over 120 trials on a rolling-origin validation scheme. Probability calibration with isotonic regression before the scores reach the CRM.
projects.results: Recall at the top two deciles reached 71%, which is where the retention budget actually lands. The team moved from cohort offers to a prioritised daily queue and save rate improved by 14% over the previous quarter. Time from prediction to outreach dropped from four days to under twelve hours.

projects.title: VisionQC
projects.summary: Computer vision inspection for a metal-parts line, catching surface defects at 42 parts per minute on a single edge device.
projects.overview:
VisionQC replaced a manual visual inspection step on an industrial line with a two-stage vision pipeline. A detector proposes regions of interest, and a small classifier decides whether each region is a genuine defect.

The constraint that shaped everything: the line runs at 42 parts per minute, so the budget was 38 milliseconds per frame on a device with no GPU.
projects.problem: Manual inspection missed roughly one in five hairline scratches, and the misses only surfaced at the customer, which meant costly returns. The quality team needed a system that worked at line speed and produced evidence for every rejection.
projects.approach: I collected 9,000 labelled frames over six weeks with a rigged camera and a lighting shroud, then split them by production shift rather than at random so the model could not memorise one lighting condition. A YOLOv8-nano detector handles region proposals, and a quantised MobileNetV3 classifier scores each crop. Both models were distilled and exported to ONNX Runtime for the edge device, with a confidence threshold tuned to the cost asymmetry of a missed defect.
projects.datasetInfo: 9,000 annotated frames (14,200 bounding boxes) across three defect classes and a hard-negative set of 2,400 near-miss surfaces. Split by shift: 6,300 train / 1,350 validation / 1,350 test. Augmentation covered lighting variation, blur and rotation.
projects.modelInfo: YOLOv8-nano (region proposal, INT8 quantised) paired with MobileNetV3-Small (defect classification). 4.1 MB total on device, 38 ms end-to-end inference on a Jetson Orin Nano.
projects.results: Defect recall reached 96% on the held-out shift split with 2.1% false positives. Scrap escapes to the customer fell to near zero, and every rejection now stores the frame and the score so quality engineers can audit a decision days later.

projects.title: AskDocs
projects.summary: A retrieval-augmented assistant that answers policy questions over 12,000 internal documents with citations on every claim.
projects.overview:
AskDocs is an internal assistant for a regulated insurance client. Staff ask policy questions in plain language and receive an answer with the exact clause it came from.

The design rule was blunt: no citation, no answer. An assistant that sounds confident and cites nothing is worse than a search box in a regulated environment.
projects.problem: Policy answers were spread across twelve thousand documents, four formats and three languages. Staff routed routine questions to a compliance mailbox, which carried a two-day turnaround and a growing backlog.
projects.approach: I built a chunking and embedding pipeline with layout-aware extraction so tables and clauses stayed intact. Retrieval is hybrid — BM25 plus dense vectors — re-ranked by a cross-encoder. Answers are generated only from retrieved passages, and an abstention rule sends low-confidence questions to a human instead of guessing. A weekly audit samples 40 answers for faithfulness.
projects.datasetInfo: 12,400 documents (PDF, DOCX, HTML), 210k chunks after layout-aware splitting, 4 languages. Evaluation set: 600 questions authored with the compliance team plus 150 adversarial unanswerable questions.
projects.modelInfo: Embeddings from a multilingual sentence-transformer at 384 dimensions, Cross-Encoder re-ranker, and a hosted instruction model for answer synthesis. Vector index in pgvector, retrieval budget of 6 passages per answer.
projects.results: Faithfulness on the audit set reached 92%, and answer correctness 88%. Routine questions now resolve in under a minute, and the compliance mailbox volume dropped by 61% in the first quarter after rollout.

projects.title: DemandLens
projects.summary: Weekly demand forecasting for 1,800 retail SKUs that cut planner overrides and freed working capital.
projects.overview:
DemandLens forecasts weekly demand per SKU per store for a grocery chain, and explains each forecast with the drivers behind it.

Forecasting projects fail on trust, not on accuracy. Planners override anything they do not understand, so half of the work went into a driver breakdown that sits next to every number.
projects.problem: Planner intuition plus a spreadsheet moving average was producing a 24% error on seasonal SKUs, tying up stock in the wrong stores while popular lines ran out on weekends.
projects.approach: I wrote a global gradient-boosted forecaster with local seasonal features — lags, rolling windows, holiday calendars, promo flags, price elasticity and weather. Hierarchical reconciliation keeps store-level predictions consistent with category totals. Backtesting used a rolling origin across 78 weeks, and I benchmarked against the incumbent spreadsheet and against a tuned Prophet baseline before proposing the switch.
projects.datasetInfo: Three years of weekly transactions across 1,800 SKUs and 62 stores (5.6M rows), plus promotion calendars, price history and local weather. Holiday and festival effects encoded per region.
projects.modelInfo: LightGBM global model (one model per category) with quantile objectives for P10/P50/P90 intervals, reconciled with MinT across the store-category hierarchy.
projects.results: Weighted MAPE improved from 24% to 8.4%, cut stockouts on top-100 SKUs by a third, and planner overrides fell from 41% of SKUs to 12% as the driver panels built confidence in the numbers.

projects.title: VoxSort
projects.summary: Sentiment and topic intelligence over 340k customer reviews, routing issues to product owners automatically.
projects.overview:
VoxSort reads every customer review, tags sentiment and topic, and routes recurring issues to the product owner responsible for that surface.

Sentiment alone was not useful. Knowing that 8% of reviews were negative changed nothing; knowing that they clustered around one broken checkout flow changed the roadmap.
projects.problem: Product teams sampled a few hundred reviews by hand each month. Real regressions hid in the long tail, and the categories people used were inconsistent between teams.
projects.approach: I fine-tuned a multilingual transformer for sentiment, then layered unsupervised topic discovery with embedding clustering so the taxonomy came from the data instead of a workshop. Topics are labelled by a human once, then tracked over time with drift alerts when a cluster grows faster than its baseline.
projects.datasetInfo: 340k reviews across four languages spanning 31 months, deduplicated and language-tagged. Labelled subset: 18,000 reviews with double annotation; inter-annotator agreement 0.86 Cohen's kappa.
projects.modelInfo: Fine-tuned multilingual transformer (sentiment, 3 classes) plus UMAP + HDBSCAN clustering over sentence embeddings for topics. Weekly drift detection with population stability index on topic shares.
projects.results: Macro F1 of 0.91 on the held-out set, 34 stable topics discovered without manual taxonomy work, and a checkout defect surfaced eleven days before it appeared in support ticket volume.

projects.title: CreditLens
projects.summary: A low-latency risk score served in 45 ms, with drift monitoring that catches decay before it reaches decisions.
projects.overview:
CreditLens scores loan applications in real time for a mid-market lender, replacing a rule engine that had grown to 340 hand-tuned conditions.

The engineering half mattered as much as the modelling half: a score that takes two seconds is a score that nobody uses, and an unmonitored score quietly writes worse loans.
projects.problem: The rule engine was opaque, hard to audit and could not be tuned without a release. Approval rates were conservative and default detection lagged by two quarters.
projects.approach: I built the feature pipeline on a streaming aggregator, trained a gradient-boosted model with monotonic constraints on the features regulators care about, and wrapped it in a FastAPI service with p99 latency headroom. Every decision logs its features and score for audit, and population stability plus realised-default monitoring runs weekly.
projects.datasetInfo: 2.1M historical applications across 40 months with 96 features: bureau attributes, bank-statement aggregates, device and application timing signals. Strict out-of-time validation on the most recent nine months.
projects.modelInfo: LightGBM with monotonic constraints on six regulatory features, isotonic probability calibration, and a fairness audit across protected groups before every release.
projects.results: ROC-AUC of 0.89 out-of-time against 0.81 for the rule engine, approval rate up 6 points with no change in realised default rate, and p99 scoring latency of 45 ms.

projects.title: Segment 360
projects.summary: Behavioural segmentation for a D2C brand that replaced demographic buckets with eight actionable groups.
projects.overview:
Segment 360 rebuilt how a direct-to-consumer brand thinks about its customers, moving from four demographic buckets to eight behavioural segments grounded in purchase rhythm, category spread and price sensitivity.

It is the least technical project here and possibly the most useful: the segmentation survived because it changed weekly campaign structure, not because the clustering was clever.
projects.problem: Every campaign targeted the same broad audience. Retention spend was proportional to customer count rather than customer value, and there was no shared vocabulary for describing the customer base.
projects.approach: I engineered behavioural features over a two-year transaction window, selected K with silhouette and stability scoring, and validated segments against held-out future behaviour. Segment profiles were then reviewed with marketing and renamed into language the team would actually use. A Streamlit app lets the team inspect and export any segment daily.
projects.datasetInfo: 620k customers, 4.1M orders across 26 months, plus web session aggregates and support interactions. Features standardised and winsorised at the 1st and 99th percentiles.
projects.modelInfo: K-Prototypes over mixed numeric and categorical features with 8 clusters, chosen via silhouette score and bootstrap stability across 40 resamples.
projects.results: Silhouette of 0.61 with stable segments across resamples. Retargeting the two high-value segments lifted campaign ROI by 27%, and campaign briefing time dropped from days to hours.

projects.title: Readmit Guard
projects.summary: A 30-day readmission risk model with a care-team interface designed for nurses, not for analysts.
projects.overview:
Readmit Guard identifies patients at high risk of returning within 30 days and surfaces the specific factors a discharge nurse can act on before the patient leaves.

The interface was the hard part. A floating-point score means nothing at a ward desk, so the model output is expressed as risk band plus the two modifiable drivers that move it most.
projects.problem: Discharge planning relied on a checklist that flagged far too many patients to be useful. Nurses ignored the flag, and readmission rates stayed flat for two years.
projects.approach: I worked with clinicians to define which features were modifiable before discharge versus fixed history, then trained a calibrated gradient-boosted model on the modifiable set for the intervention view and the full set for scoring. Validation was by hospital site to avoid the model learning institutional quirks, and threshold selection used cost-sensitive analysis of nursing time.
projects.datasetInfo: 84k admissions across three hospital sites and 19 months, with 128 features from vitals, labs, medication history and prior utilisation. Site-based split: two sites for training, one held out entirely.
projects.modelInfo: Gradient-boosted trees with class weighting, probability calibration, and a cost-sensitive decision threshold tuned to available nursing hours rather than to accuracy.
projects.results: Recall of 0.87 at the operating threshold, 30-day readmissions down 11% on the pilot ward, and nurse-flagged false positives below 3% — the number that decided whether the model stayed in the workflow.

projects.title: GridPulse
projects.summary: An autoencoder that watches 3.4k energy meters and flags anomalies that rules-based thresholds always missed.
projects.overview:
GridPulse monitors substation-level energy readings and flags anomalies — meter tampering, sensor faults and unusual load behaviour — without any labelled examples of the anomalies themselves.

With no fraud labels to train on, the whole approach had to be unsupervised and the evaluation had to be built from a small set of confirmed historical cases.
projects.problem: A threshold alerting system produced 400 alerts per week, almost all of them expected seasonal load. Operators stopped reading them, and genuine meter faults sat open for weeks.
projects.approach: I trained a temporal autoencoder on normal consumption patterns per substation, using reconstruction error as an anomaly score. Alerts are clustered into incidents rather than fired per meter, and ranked by persistence so a one-minute blip does not wake anybody. I validated against 61 confirmed historical incidents the field team had documented.
projects.datasetInfo: 3,400 meters at 15-minute resolution over 18 months (98M readings), joined with weather and calendar features. Evaluation used 61 confirmed incidents plus a synthetic fault injection set.
projects.modelInfo: LSTM-based sequence autoencoder per substation cluster, with a per-cluster anomaly threshold set from the reconstruction-error distribution and a 30-minute persistence rule before alerting.
projects.results: Alert volume fell from 400 to 46 per week while recall on confirmed incidents stayed at 0.90. Mean time to detect a genuine meter fault dropped from nine days to under four hours.
